entry.title: Revisiting Autoresearch for Scientific Discovery
entry.content:
Methods

Models

Paper Models Agent setup
Fork-and-Flush GPT-5.6-terra (high); GPT-5.5 (extra-high) for VLIW and tinyCIFAR. Copilot CLI; four branches per fork.
Forgetting DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Pi; four communicating agents with periodic resets.
SLA GPT-5.5 or Opus 4.8. Codex or Claude Code; stateless Advisor and Workers.
CCTS Gemini 2.0 Flash. Program generation and concept extraction; statistical parent selection.
MIRA / MIRA-AC Qwen3.6-27B for MIRA-AC; GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 Astra in untrained MIRA studies. Trained decision policy and shared critic; fixed curator and fresh Codex executors.
IdeaScientist Qwen3.6-27B; base variants include Gemma-4-31B and GPT-OSS-120B. GRPO-trained ideation roles; fixed orchestrator.
DuoDiscover Opus 5 with Sonnet 5 helper; Gemini 3.8 Flash in additional runs. Claude Code or Antigravity; four Workers by default.

Evaluation sample complexity

One example per paper. An evaluation means scoring a candidate with the task evaluator; proposals, internal tests and final grading are counted separately.

Paper Selected example Evaluation count Where proposals and evaluations differ
Fork-and-Flush Polyomino, Frontier-CS #0; 25,000 credits/run. Whole-run total not reported. An agent episode can submit for grading multiple times. Four branches do not imply four evals. The public task config lists 70 test cases per full suite; those are cases within an eval, not 70 new candidates. The paper’s search wrapper is unavailable for verification.
Forgetting AHC014, four-agent continue-vs-forget ablation. 30 prefix + 30 continuation proposals per agent: 240 proposals across the team, including the shared prefix. Completed eval total not reported. The harness scores candidates after an agent returns; the agent is told not to run the judge itself. Empty turns can produce no candidate. The proposal budget alone does not establish how many candidates reached the judge.
SLA VLIW, Codex/GPT-5.5; 1B-token budget. 3 Workers × 3 local trials = 9 scheduled trials per full Advisor epoch. Whole-run evaluator-call total not reported. The harness evaluates the returned candidate outside the Worker. Nine trials are not evidence of nine completed evals: failure, retry and caching behavior require the implementation or logs, which are not released in the official repository.
CCTS Circle packing, n = 26; main Gemini-2.0-Flash comparison. 25 search iterations; the defined loop schedules one child-fitness evaluation per iteration. This gives 25 scheduled calls to the program-level evaluator, not an audited invocation total. Seed evaluations, failed-generation retries and optimization inside the generated program are not itemized. The 60 runs are independent replicates.
MIRA / MIRA-AC BNLearn causal discovery; one 14–34-node graph. Up to 20 iteration-end SHD scores + a final graph-scoring stage, derived from the protocol. Separately, at most n interventions on an n-node task. The executor cannot query graph accuracy during a work order. The harness reports SHD after each completed iteration. BIC diagnostics and interventions are separate queries, so the 20-decision cap does not cap every kind of evaluation at 20.
IdeaScientist One proposal-generation run, then the standard evaluation script. In-loop review count is adaptive. For a valid final report, the default scorer makes 5 logical rubric calls, before retries and optional metrics. The 100-turn orchestrator cap is not a review cap: a turn can spawn multiple sub-agents. Reviews use literature and judge reasoning; the proposed scientific experiment is not executed. The five final calls are outside the search loop.
DuoDiscover vLLM serving on 8×B200, 20 hours, initially four agents. About 90 candidate edits; 7 full true evaluations, including the final combined edit. Claude Code uses 12 full evals. Cheap yardsticks screen candidates first; their invocation total is not reported for this run. One full eval bundles correctness checks and a serving-load sweep over four metrics (~85 min). Those metrics are not four separate candidate evals.
Code checks and counting details

IdeaScientist is directly traceable in code. The runner loops over tool calls within each orchestrator turn and executes the requested sub-agents. A reviewer invocation can itself take several LLM turns. For a valid report and available comparison records, evaluate_run requests five rubrics: proposal quality, relevance, novelty against all work, novelty before the cutoff, and reference-grounded similarity. Each is one logical judge call. The JSON parser retry loop allows up to three attempts per rubric; transport retries and separately requested metrics add further calls.

A test suite is another level of counting. For SLA’s VLIW task, the upstream submission tests run eight randomized correctness simulations and one cached cycle measurement during a successful full test invocation. Several speed-threshold assertions reuse that measurement. This describes the public benchmark, not a verified copy of SLA’s private evaluator wrapper.

Release coverage. The SLA repository contains the preprint only; the DuoDiscover repository contains its project page and assets. I did not locate official search implementations for Fork-and-Flush, Forgetting, CCTS or MIRA. Their entries therefore describe the paper’s protocol, not code-verified call totals. Benchmark source alone cannot establish a paper’s complete search budget.

entry.title: Revisiting PPO for LLM Post-Training
entry.content:
Recent PPO work revisits how trajectories are sampled, how the critic estimates returns, and how policy updates handle distribution mismatch. Mapping these changes onto the training loop makes the methods easier to compare.

Revisiting PPO

PPO gives the actor and critic different jobs. The actor learns which actions to make more likely. The critic estimates the return expected from the current prompt and generated prefix, providing a baseline for the actor’s update.

Two updates, different interventions

For actor $\pi_ heta$ and critic $V_\phi$, write $\psi_ heta= abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a\mid s)$. Their updates expose the main components:

\[ egin{aligned} g_{\mathrm{actor}}&=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\!\left[m\,\hat A\,(w\psi_ heta-c(s)) ight],\[4pt] L_V&=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\!\left[m^V\omega_x\,\ell(V_\phi(s),Y) ight]. \end{aligned}\]

$\mathcal D$: sampled trajectories · $m,m^V$: masks and aggregation · $\hat A$: advantage · $w$: probability correction · $c$: score correction · $\omega_x,Y$: critic weight and target. This is a component map: clipping enters through effective weights/masks; KL terms are omitted.

Work Main intervention
SAO $\mathcal D$: one rollout per prompt; $\hat A$: skip-observation GAE; $w$: strict token masking; more frequent critic updates.
FlashREINFORCE $\hat A_i=R_i- ar R_{\mathrm{batch}}$; single rollouts, sequence admission, per-trajectory averaging; no $L_V$.
AC2 $\hat A_i=v_i- ar v$, $Y= ar v$; critic-ready problems use $v_i=V(s\cdot c_i)$ for unfinished chunks.
TEMPO $\hat A_t=V(y_{\mathrm{complete}})-V(s_t)$; periodically recalibrate $V$ on labeled data.
Score Centering $c(s)=\mathbb E_{a\sim\mu(\cdot\mid s)}[w\psi_ heta]$: center the weighted score under the sampler $\mu$.
Decoupled PPO Separate $ u/\mu$ for behavior correction from $\pi_ heta/ u$ for PPO clipping; $ u$ is a recent policy.
EasyPPO $\omega_x\propto1/\max(\hat\sigma_x,\varepsilon)$; $m^V$ retains truncated samples; smaller critic minibatches.

For complete terminal-return PPO with $\gamma=\lambda=1$, $\hat A_t=R-V_{\mathrm{old}}(s_t)$. Reward centering changes $\hat A$; score centering changes the gradient term $c(s)$.

These papers use the critic in different ways. A baseline reduces variance after we observe an outcome. A learned evaluator supplies feedback when a real outcome is unavailable or expensive. The second role asks much more of the model.

What makes TTT special?

One problem, many attempts

Here, sample = 1 at the task level. We adapt to one target problem, rather than training over a broad collection of unrelated questions. We can still generate many candidates and evaluate them on many cases. All those attempts serve the same search.

This also changes the input distribution. Each successful revision becomes a possible starting point for the next attempt. The model learns while the problem in front of it changes.

We keep the best of all attempts

At the end, we want the strongest verified solution found anywhere in the history. The objective is closer to:

\[\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{1\leq k\leq N} S(c_k) ight],\]

where later candidates can depend on earlier results. Repeatedly producing a good existing solution helps average reward but adds little to that maximum. We need enough reliability to keep the search moving, alongside a willingness to try changes that might fail.

Discovery needs depth

An experiment often reveals what to try next. Generating a large batch before receiving feedback delays that process: every candidate in the batch starts from the same available history.

With a fixed candidate budget, larger batches leave fewer rounds to learn from the results. Smaller batches give later attempts more opportunities to build on earlier discoveries.

Parallel exploration still matters, and smaller batches can make updates noisier. The question is how much breadth we can afford before sacrificing useful feedback depth.
